articles.title: A new axis of malice threatens the global order
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
When Russia began using jet-powered Geran-4 drones against Ukraine in May, the battlespace began to shift in the Kremlin’s favour. They were much faster than Russia’s earlier, propeller-driven models, putting huge strain on Ukraine’s defences. But the new weapons signified a shift with global dimensions too. They were the product of intensifying, often secret, collaboration by an axis of autocracies with overlapping goals: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

Once Ukrainian forces were able to inspect an intact Geran-4, they found it was based on Iran’s delta-winged Shahed suicide-drone, and upgraded with Russian-designed modules including a new warhead and optical navigation system (see diagram). The jet engine and anti-jamming antenna came from China, as did many other electronic parts. Internal markings showed that it was made at Russia’s Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan, where as many as 25,000 North Koreans are thought to work in a complex packed with Chinese industrial machinery.

Collusion by this axis of malice goes far beyond the Geran-4. Its members are sharing military technology and expertise in ways that are altering the military balance of Europe, the Middle East and Asia. The network of manufacturers, traders, banks and ships that underpin collaboration is growing more sophisticated and resilient. And deepening economic ties are making the axis less susceptible to Western pressure. All that is making it harder to enforce UN and Western sanctions.

One consequence is that Western and Ukrainian officials believe North Korea has obtained from Russia much of the drone technology in—and expertise in using—the Geran-4 and other weapons. That has been part of a pay-off for North Korea providing arms and some 16,000 troops to help fight Ukraine. Similar drone components and tactics are being used by Iran in the Middle East, too. Iran continues to send drone engineers to Russia, long after sharing initial Shahed designs, according to Ukrainian officials. “They are still going back and forth, exchanging knowledge,” says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, a Ukrainian presidential aide on sanctions policy.

China, meanwhile, has been regularly sending military officers and technicians to Russian facilities that produce and operate military drones. China’s capacity to manufacture drones is unrivalled. But it lacks combat experience: its last war was against Vietnam in 1979. So it is hoovering up Russian knowledge to improve its own drone designs and tactics, hoping to gain an edge in a potential conflict over Taiwan. Russia, Iran and North Korea, in turn, are likely to rely increasingly on China’s AI stack for cyber-attacks, disinformation campaigns and autonomous weapons.

The axis is tilting the global nuclear balance as well. While China supplies Russia with machinery, drone parts and other “dual-use” items (with civilian and military applications), the Kremlin is helping it to build a missile-warning system and quieter nuclear-missile submarines, according to Western officials. Russia and China are also now enabling North Korea’s drive to become a fully fledged nuclear power. And covert support from Russia, China and North Korea has helped Iran to survive its conflict with America and Israel.

This global realignment was the backdrop for a showy trilateral meeting on November 19th between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at a summit of Asia-Pacific powers in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Some pundits have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945. But officials involved did not expect any breakthroughs. The axis, meanwhile, grows stronger.

The nature of the axis coalition is debated by Western officials and scholars. Some see it as an emerging alliance of revisionist autocracies that threaten democracy worldwide. They liken it to the Eastern bloc in the cold war or the Axis alliance in the second world war. A book published this year by the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, a hawkish American think-tank, counted 600-plus instances of axis security co-operation in 2019-25, with a marked increase since 2022. Bradley Bowman, its lead author, argues that this co-operation in some ways surpasses that of the original Axis powers. It is “gaining momentum, making each adversary more formidable than they would be otherwise”.

Sceptics see the grouping more as a temporary “axis of convenience” without common long-term goals or ironclad mutual-defence commitments. They warn that exaggerating the threat could push the four countries closer together. Although China has had a mutual-defence treaty with North Korea since 1961, China’s commitment to that is questionable. Russia signed a new one with the North Koreans in 2024 and a more limited “strategic partnership” with Iran last year. This collection of bilateral links thus falls well short of a formal alliance like NATO, each member of which is formally committed to defend any other that comes under attack.

A closer parallel might be the Axis powers in the three years before the second world war began. They co-ordinated on foreign policy, intelligence and military affairs but largely on an ad hoc basis until Germany and Italy signed their “Pact of Steel” in 1939. A tripartite defence treaty including Japan followed in 1940. Another analogy is a syndicate of mafia bosses, who co-operate and compete simultaneously. What unites them is disregard for the law and reliance on underground networks of transport and finance.

Although quadrilateral axis meetings are not thought to occur, the four often vote in unison at the UN, helping to shield each other from sanctions or other actions. China, Russia and Iran also co-ordinate formally via international organisations such as the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation and the BRICs (which includes Brazil, Russia, India and China). But more often the four countries support each other in transactional, bilateral and covert ways. Spying on and stealing from each other is routine. And they often withhold their best military technology, sharing enough to prevent defeat, but not to secure victory.

Binding them together is a common desire to challenge American global leadership and to dominate their respective regions. “I don’t think they have in their minds an alternative order. They’re just trying to disrupt the US order, and then they’re trying to capitalise on that,” says Victor Cha, a former American national-security official now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a think-tank in Washington. But what began as transactional alignments has laid “the infrastructure for something that could last longer”, he says. That like-mindedness can show in their propaganda as well; state media in Russia and China in particular routinely share content with one another and, when it suits them, spread each other’s messages.

Axis members still have different and often conflicting goals. China, for instance, worries that Russia’s growing influence in North Korea is emboldening its leader, Kim Jong Un. In return for his help on Ukraine, the Kremlin has provided economic support and military tech that have helped him bolster his conventional and nuclear arsenals. That troubles China, which has long sought to avert another war on its north-eastern border. Were North Korea to obtain a fully fledged nuclear arsenal, China fears that it could provoke an American attack or prompt South Korea and Japan, both American allies, to develop nuclear weapons that would target China, as well as Mr Kim’s territory.

And yet, in the last year, China has revitalised its relations with Mr Kim, dropping public objections to his nuclear weapons programme, expanding cross-border transport links and lifting trade restrictions. As North Korea’s economy revives, it has more to spend on nuclear weapons. And its conventional forces are becoming more of a threat to South Korea as battle-hardened North Korean troops return home and adopt technology and tactics honed in Ukraine and the Middle East.

China and Russia have divergent aims and strategies in the Middle East too. China wants to stabilise the region, where it now has close relations with Gulf Arab states that Iran has bombed. Many of them supply China with oil or gas. Concerned that high energy prices are worsening its economic slowdown, China also hopes to open up the Strait of Hormuz. Russia, by contrast, seeks to destabilise the region, push up oil prices and gain leverage in negotiations with America over Ukraine.

But Messrs Xi and Putin share enough common interests in the Middle East for their actions to be complementary. Neither wants a fully nuclear-armed Iran. Yet they are anxious to ensure that its regime does not collapse (and possibly be replaced with a Western-leaning alternative). They also see the war there as a useful way to divert America’s military resources and undermine public support for its military intervention abroad.

The axis’s security interests appear to be compatible enough that their co-operation across a range of military technologies is deepening. When Russia started using North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles in 2023, they often missed targets or exploded mid-air. Russia has since made them more accurate and manoeuvrable by adding new components, including a Chinese-made receiver connecting it to Russian and Chinese satellite networks. The explosive charge has also changed to hexogen, which is more potent and made in Russia, according to Ukrainian experts. And the KN-23 can now carry cluster warheads, which inflict damage over a wider area. Those and other improvements appear to have flowed back to North Korea, which conducted a series of missile tests in recent weeks.

Iran’s missiles have been getting more accurate too. The ones that hit Qatar’s gas-liquefaction facilities at Ras Laffan precisely destroyed two “cold boxes”, the most vital and hard-to-repair parts of the plant. Iran was also able to strike American radars, aircraft and facilities across the Gulf. The British-American base of Diego Garcia, in the Indian Ocean, has been targeted too, as have American warships off Iran.

Although many of Iran’s missiles are based on old North Korean designs, it no longer needs outside expertise in building them and has developed its own generation of solid-fuel missiles that can be fired quickly. Even so, their recent accuracy may derive from Chinese and Russian intelligence helping to identify targets, according to Western officials. They believe Iran has access to a Chinese surveillance satellite. And perhaps more important, Iran (like Russia and North Korea) is now able to use China’s BeiDou satellite-navigation system to help guide its missiles.

Iran also still depends on specialist machinery, components and materials from abroad, especially China. The clearest support is through Chinese supplies of precursor chemicals for solid fuel, notably sodium perchlorate. A Chinese ship carrying the chemical exploded last year in an Iranian port. And Chinese ships continued to deliver it this year. There is also evidence of Chinese components being supplied to Iran’s proxy militias, including Hizbullah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen. Valuable details came from the contents of four containers seized in July in Aden, with Chinese cargo bound for a Houthi-controlled port. Analysis by Conflict Armament Research, a think-tank, shows it included parts for Iranian missiles. Those components appear to have been custom-made by a Chinese firm.

Whether China’s government is complicit in such exports is hard to determine. It denies supplying weapons to Iran, Russia or North Korea. But much of what it exports to all three are dual-use items, such as electronics and industrial machinery. Those exports sustain their military programmes and their broader economies, while Chinese consumer goods help to pacify their domestic populations. Russia, in particular, relies on imports from China, which are expected to reach $120bn-130bn this year, an 80-90% increase since 2021. While Western governments forbid the sale to Russia of dual-use items needed to make weapons, China is believed to supply as much as 90% of them.

Even if some of this trade is done without the Chinese government’s knowledge, many Western officials believe that (given its formidable surveillance capabilities) it either secretly approves or consciously turns a blind eye to exports that it knows will be used for military purposes. The Geran-4’s original engine, for instance, was made by a Chinese firm whose website specifies that it can be used in cruise missiles and drones. China tightened export controls on drone engines in October. But Ukrainian officials believe that Russia has already localised production at Alabuga.

Russian and Iranian weapons also often contain Western electronic components. But they are mostly imported via a complex network of trading firms and proxies, many of which are based in China or Hong Kong. China refuses to enforce Western sanctions imposed on dozens of such firms for supplying items for military use to Russia, Iran or North Korea. This year, China introduced rules that would penalise foreign companies and individuals for observing export controls or sanctions imposed on Chinese firms by other governments.

China’s big banks still generally comply with Western sanctions, fearing suspension from US dollar payments and clearing systems. But China has built a network of alternative financial institutions and mechanisms that is largely insulated from Western sanctions. It has also accelerated efforts to “de-dollarise” its trade with Russia, Iran and other targets of sanctions. More than 95% of Russia’s trade with China is now conducted in yuan or roubles, compared with about 25% five years ago.

That enables the oil trade that sustains the axis (see chart). China imports about 90% of Iran’s oil exports and roughly half of Russia’s. Since China mostly pays in yuan, Iran and Russia can use those revenues to finance purchases of Chinese dual-use tech. And the oil is mostly transported via a “shadow fleet” of ageing tankers, many of which are owned and managed through shell companies in Hong Kong and mainland China (as well as Dubai). Those tactics were pioneered by Iran but are increasingly used by Russia. As a result, the shadow fleet has expanded to more than 3,000 ships from about 200 in 2022. North Korea, meanwhile, imports almost all of its oil overland from China and Russia.

Transport links are thickening too. China and Russia are building a new cross-border gas pipeline that is due to open in 2027; they have opened new road and rail bridges and are planning new railway crossings. And they co-operate closely on expanding the Northern Sea Route through the Arctic. Since September, Russia and China have both opened new cross-border road bridges to North Korea. Russian and Chinese links to Iran, meanwhile, provide a window on the outside world. Iranian airlines still fly between Tehran, Moscow and Shanghai. Shipping between Russia and Iran via the Caspian Sea has surged this year. So has rail freight from China to Iran via Central Asia.

Closer axis collusion is not inevitable. If the wars in Iran and Ukraine end, demand for military technology may wane, along with the trade in oil under sanctions. With fewer incentives to co-operate, mutual suspicions could deepen. Axis members fear becoming dependent on each other and, given the opportunity, would like to expand commercial links with the West. Circumventing sanctions adds costs and Chinese companies, in particular, fear losing access to rich-world markets. With co-ordinated action, and strong leadership from the White House, that might give America and its allies some leverage. For now, though, the axis represents a challenge to which the West has no good response. ■

articles.title: How China continues to evade America’s tech-export rules
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
“WE WILL NOT let anybody have them other than the United States,” declared Donald Trump last year of Nvidia’s most advanced chips—an essential tool in the race to develop superpowered AI. To enforce the pledge, his administration maintained rules restricting sales of certain types of semiconductor. Anything less, a Republican congressmen said, would be as foolhardy as handing Iran weapons-grade uranium.

Yet all the while, it turns out, a torrent of Nvidia’s nattiest chips was flowing to China or to middlemen who made them available to Chinese AI firms. Although America is now trying to plug the sieve of leaks, China’s efforts to obtain the latest technology are continuing by other means. What is more, China’s own chipmaking industry is advancing so fast that it may soon render America’s controls moot.

The scale of the leakage has been revealed by the downfall of Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s boss. While he was having an affair with a suspected Chinese agent named Alice Huang, the firm she worked at, Megaspeed, became the biggest buyer of Nvidia’s chips in South-East Asia. Many of these seem to have ended up in China, in breach of America’s regulations; others power data centres in the region used by Chinese clients—a set-up that had been legal, although this week American officials hastily revised their rules to curb it. Alibaba, a Chinese tech giant, is Megaspeed’s biggest customer and one of its biggest creditors.

Since America first started restricting the export of advanced chips in 2020, Chinese firms have devised an ever-shifting set of workarounds to access “compute” (processing power). Huawei, a Chinese tech giant, was singled out by American sanctions that year, cutting it off from components made by TSMC, Taiwan’s biggest chipmaker. Yet when TechInsights, a research firm, dissected one of Huawei’s Ascend 910B processors, which are intended for use in AI, they found chips made by TSMC. According to SemiAnalysis, a consultancy, Huawei bought some $500m-worth of advanced TSMC chips through Sophgo, a Chinese chip-designer. (Sophgo says it had no dealings with Huawei.)

When the restrictions were broadened to all Chinese firms, many resorted to smuggling. In 2024 the Wall Street Journal detailed a “barely concealed” chip-trafficking network, including a student paid $600 to sneak Nvidia chips into China in his suitcase. But it was not just small-time bootlegging. America’s Department of Justice claims a co-founder of Supermicro, an American server-maker, and two other men conspired to sneak billions-worth of AI kit into China between 2024 and 2025 (the co-founder denies it). The trio allegedly ordered chips through a South-East Asian shell company, then repackaged them into unmarked boxes that were sent on to China. Security footage shows one of them placing fake equipment in the original packaging to make it seem like the chips had never left South-East Asia, to trick both compliance staff at Supermicro and American officials.

No one is quite sure how much smuggling there has been. SemiAnalysis thinks roughly 1.5 gigawatts of compute, which is equivalent to about 1m restricted Nvidia chips, have ended up in China. This stockpile is especially useful for Chinese firms since access to it “can’t be cut off”, notes a former China analyst at the CIA. But it is not big enough to satisfy China’s ever greater hunger for compute. Smuggled chips provide around 22% of its AI data-centre capacity, according to the Institute for Progress (IFP), a think-tank. Moreover, smuggling routes are becoming inconvenient. Since Malaysia tightened permitting rules for high-end semiconductor shipments last year, smuggling to China plummeted, Malaysian officials insist.

An alternative workaround is to exploit loopholes in the rules. AI processors depend on high-bandwidth memory (HBM), stacks of memory chips that China cannot yet make in large numbers. Before America banned their sale to China in late 2024, Huawei stockpiled some 13m HBM stacks, enough for 1.6m of its advanced AI chips, reckons SemiAnalysis. Since then, it says, Huawei has kept up supplies by getting HBM chips grafted onto other, outmoded chips. The combined product does not exceed the technical thresholds specified in America’s rules and so can be shipped to China legally, where it is disassembled again to get at the HBM chips.

An even bigger loophole has involved renting, rather than buying, computing power. Instead of trying to spirit restricted chips across borders, Chinese firms have simply been making use of them from afar. Remotely accessed capacity makes up a quarter of China’s total AI compute, estimates IFP. This, too, flows through South-East Asia. After Singapore limited data-centre construction for lack of space and power, projects gravitated to Malaysia, where data-centre capacity has grown 100-fold in the past five years. It now boasts 55 big data centres, with another 62 in the pipeline. Taiwan, the source of most of the world’s high-end chips, exports a majority of them to America and Mexico (where they are assembled into goods bound for America). Exclude those two countries, and Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand absorb more than half of the rest (see chart 1), an astonishing share of global demand that is clearly not catering simply to domestic consumers.

Oracle, an American cloud-computing firm, for instance, runs data centres in South-East Asia that work with ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, which also owns an advanced AI lab. articles.title: America has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
PAOLO DECUZZI has spent decades trying to get tiny devices to do big things. The biomedical engineer, based at the Italian Institute of Technology in Genoa, has devised an assortment of nanotechnologies that aim to deliver drugs more effectively. To turn these inventions into working medical treatments, he has long collaborated with American scientists on projects funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the largest funder of biomedical research in the world. But last year the NIH abruptly suspended research to study a microscopic plate Dr Decuzzi had invented to deliver drugs directly into arthritic joints. He estimates that another one, intended for cancer patients, has been set back by as much as two years.

Many researchers have experienced something similar. In the fiscal year ending September 2024 the NIH gave an estimated $400m to 3,600 collaborating foreign scientists. It was a fraction of the nearly $35bn in grants the agency doled out, but an easy target for the Trump administration as it cut NIH projects broadly. The result is that America’s system for funding international research has been gutted.

Extensive internal NIH data shared with The Economist on the condition of anonymity shows the scale of the change. In the fiscal years 2022-2024 the agency awarded an average of 2,040 grants a year to projects with foreign components. The average for 2025 and 2026 was 38% lower (see chart 1). In its purported pursuit of transparency and accountability, the administration has disrupted valuable science and inadvertently made its spending more inscrutable.

For all of America’s science dominance, some resources cannot easily be found at home. Dr Decuzzi’s microparticles, for example, cannot be bought off the shelf. Conducting clinical trials on rare diseases often requires enrolling patients from countries where cases are more common.

Such collaborations have long been governed by strict conditions, at least on paper. The existing guidelines were blown apart in May 2025, however, when the NIH barred American universities from using an established scheme to pass grant money to their overseas partners. Projects that already had funding could continue, but those waiting for their next yearly instalment were suspended until the following spring. For over a year, the NIH essentially shut off its means of funding new international research partnerships.

The architect of this overhaul is Jay Bhattacharya, who has led the NIH since April 2025. He is also a vocal proponent of the covid lab-leak hypothesis, which contends that the virus escaped from the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China. (America’s National Intelligence Council has concluded, albeit with low confidence, that a natural origin was more likely.) The lab had previously received NIH funding, which troubles Dr Bhattacharya. “The goal”, he said in a 2025 interview with Christianity Today, an Evangelical magazine, is “to put those foreign collaborations on more solid footing so that a Wuhan situation never happens again”.

Concerns about oversight are not unfounded. After the pandemic the institute in Wuhan refused to co-operate with its American research partner, leaving investigators unable to retrieve records of NIH-funded research that could help establish the virus’s origins. In 2023 the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a congressional watchdog, found that the NIH “had not taken near-term steps to manage risks” associated with funding research abroad, and made recommendations that the agency then acted on.

The Trump administration has gone much further. Although foreign grants make up a small share of NIH awards, they have suffered disproportionately. At the National Institute on Ageing grants with a foreign component fell by 49%, compared with 11% for domestic grants. At both the children’s health and biomedical imaging institutes foreign grants declined by over 40% even as domestic awards rose slightly (see chart 2). All told, grants of $5m or more that include a foreign component fell from an average of 20 in 2022-2024 to just three in 2026.

The reductions cut across nearly every institute but those studying infectious diseases and mental health saw the largest drop in the number of projects. The Economist’s analysis reveals that the number of grants whose title mentions Africa, clinical trials, children, mothers, HIV or “ageing and dementia” was roughly half that of the average during the previous three years.

For Dr Decuzzi the chaos means years of lost postdoctoral students, slower discoveries and more paperwork. “Once we have destroyed things, rebuilding is actually very difficult,” he laments. For others the consequences have been grimmer still. Dvora Joseph Davey, an epidemiologist studying HIV at the University of California in Los Angeles, has long been affiliated with the University of Cape Town. In May 2025 the NIH pulled her international funding, forcing her to end a clinical trial. She had been investigating how best to prevent HIV transmission among pregnant and breastfeeding women in a country where roughly 20% of women of reproductive age have the virus. Study participants subsequently lost access to PrEP, drugs that reduce the risk of HIV infection by 99%. Two women in her study who stopped taking the drug became infected and one of them transmitted the virus to her baby. Dr Bhattacharya calls this case “unfortunate”, but says that ensuring patient care following a grant suspension is the researchers’ responsibility.

The internal data shared with The Economist do not identify spending by country, but grant titles suggest that South Africa has been hit particularly hard. Between 2022 and 2024 a yearly average of 18 new foreign grants contained South Africa in their title. In 2026 that figure dropped to one. A separate analysis by Grant Witness, a non-profit, suggests that the focus of funded research is also changing. A comparison of grants shows that references to Africa had been removed from 184 grant abstracts in 2025 and 2026 (see chart 3). Researchers in South Africa have also been tangled up in Mr Trump’s dispute with their government over allegations of a “white genocide” against Afrikaners. In February 2025 Mr Trump halted American aid to South Africa, a restriction the NIH interpreted as applying to its research grants, too. articles.title: Can American Socialism Survive Its Success?
articles.author: Jill Lepore
articles.body_markdown:
It was American socialism’s best year ever. In 1912, the Socialist Party of America tallied a hundred and twenty thousand members, and newsstands groaned under the weight of some three hundred socialist papers and magazines, including the Kansas-based Appeal to Reason , which had three-quarters of a million subscribers and was committed to the belief that “socialism is not just a theory—it is a destiny.” Socialists were winning elections, carried to victory by voters furious at trusts and corporations and millionaires and oligarchs, whose monopoly on political power rested on a two-party system indifferent to labor’s demands and on a breathtakingly conservative Supreme Court. (In 1895, the Court declared a federal income tax to be unconstitutional; in 1905, it said the same of a law limiting the number of hours in a workday.) Year by year, socialists had gained strength. In 1910, the Milwaukee newspaperman Victor Berger, who had founded the Socialist Party with the Indiana railroad-union leader Eugene V. Debs, in 1901, became the first socialist elected to Congress: he vowed to abolish the Senate. In 1911, a socialist mayor was elected in Schenectady, New York. “We know that we cannot abolish the capitalist system in Schenectady,” he said at his inauguration. But “we can and will demonstrate to all the spirit of socialism and the application of socialist principles insofar as possible with the handicap of laws framed to establish and sustain capitalism.” (He pledged to lower trolley fares.) In 1912, Debs ran as the Socialist Party candidate for President and called for an end to “wage slavery.” Across a great striving land of fields of wheat and corn, and factories of steel and automobiles, and mines of coal and copper and iron, more than a thousand socialists held office, including fifty-six mayors (of cities as different as Berkeley, California, and Flint, Michigan), a hundred and sixty city councilmen, and a hundred and forty-five aldermen. A machinist became the mayor of St. Marys, Ohio; a railroad brakeman the mayor of New Castle, Pennsylvania. “But, comrades, it is not merely our physical growth, it is not merely our large strength upon which we congratulate ourselves,” the chairman of the Socialist Party Convention, held in Indianapolis that year, declared. “It is the fact that the Socialist Party has, at all times, remained true to its trust and carried the banner of international socialism aloft in this country.” Socialism’s moment, it seemed, had arrived.

At that convention, the Party adopted a platform that began by denouncing capitalism as a system that produced, among other evils, an “extortionate cost of living”: “Under this system the working class is exposed to poisonous conditions, to frightful and needless perils to life and limb, is walled around with court decisions, injunctions and unjust laws, and is preyed upon incessantly for the benefit of the controlling oligarchy of wealth.” The platform called for the collective ownership of everything from the railroads and the telegraph lines to mines, forests, oil wells, banks, and the currency system. It called for a shortened workday, a workweek no longer than five and a half days, a minimum wage, old-age pensions, workers’ insurance, unemployment insurance, and the abolition of child labor. It also called for a graduated federal income tax, female suffrage, and the abolition of the Senate, the Presidential veto, and the Electoral College—and, since each of the items on this last list would require amending the Constitution, for a constitutional convention.

“The socialist moment is here,” Nathan J. Robinson, the editor of the socialist magazine Current Affairs , announced this past summer, pointing to the swelling membership of the Democratic Socialists of America and to socialists’ newfound prominence: Zohran Mamdani on the cover of Time . Is it 1912 all over again?

This year, the banner of socialism is being carried by the D.S.A., whose hundred and thirty thousand members already include two U.S. representatives, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib; there are hundreds of D.S.A.-backed state and local officeholders across the country. (Bernie Sanders is a longtime socialist, but he is not a member of the D.S.A.) The D.S.A. is not a political party, but it does have a platform. Sort of. In 2017, its National Political Committee decided to replace its “priorities resolution” with a platform. Promised for 2019, it was postponed to 2021, given the D.S.A.’s “ideological diversity.” A new platform, which the D.S.A. prefers to call a “program,” was released this summer. It has much in common with the Socialist Party platform of 1912.

“We are workers fighting to transform society: to win the battle for democracy, draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic,” the program pledges, while inveighing against the existing parties: “Both are funded by the same criminal class of billionaires and war profiteers.” The program proposes, among other things, the abolition of the Senate and the replacement of the Presidency and Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress.

A number of prominent Democrats condemned the platform. On Fox News, the host Shannon Bream asked Megan Romer, a D.S.A. co-chair, to confirm some of its proposals:

Romer, who grinned and seemed almost to laugh at one point during this quiz, came across as glib and, at best, remarkably naïve. “These people are insane,” Ted Cruz tweeted.

Then came Election Day, an epic Democratic sweep that reinvigorated the Party and brought gains for socialists not seen since 1912. Six D.S.A. members—from California, Colorado, Michigan, New York, and Pennsylvania—won seats in Congress (and the two sitting D.S.A. members won reëlection). D.S.A. candidates won mayoral races in Los Angeles; Washington, D.C.; Ann Arbor, Michigan; and Providence, Rhode Island. Even socialism’s losses were triumphs. The little red scare of 2026 backfired. The D.S.A. member Angie Nixon lost her long-shot bid to unseat the Republican Ashley Moody, a U.S. senator from Florida, who had characterized the campaign as “freedom versus socialism,” but Moody’s margin of victory was just 2.9 per cent. Mamdani, speaking at the Election Night party of Kathy Hochul (no socialist she), announced the dawn of a new era: “We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again.”

The United States has no meaningful socialist party, and socialism has never overtaken either of the country’s two major political parties. This distinguishes the U.S. from every other Western democracy and would have surprised early American socialists, who pointed to a tradition of communalism stretching from the Shakers to the Owenites. In 1869, John Humphrey Noyes, the American preacher and utopian, proclaimed that “this country has been from the beginning, and especially for the last forty years, a laboratory in which Socialisms of all kinds have been experimenting.” It was as if socialism was in the soil, as American as the Revolution.

Nevertheless, socialism didn’t really come to the fore of American politics until the Panic of 1893, when, according to Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., “a vague terror went over the earth and the word socialism began to be heard.” After the railway magnate George Pullman cut workers’ wages by a quarter, Debs called for a strike, and in 1895 he was sent to prison for his role in organizing it; Victor Berger visited him, bringing a copy of “Das Kapital.” (Debs’s extraordinary life is the subject of a lively and admiring new biography, “American Socialist,” by Shawn Gude.) Debs, a Democrat, said that he had previously “heard but little of Socialism,” and he did not become a socialist until 1897, after a campaign funded by plutocrats elevated William McKinley to the White House, convincing Debs that the rich controlled politics. “Money constitutes no proper basis of civilization,” he concluded. He first ran for President in 1900, and when he ran again four years later he earned more than four times as many votes.

“If my reading of history is correct, the prophecy of Marx will be fulfilled, and America will ring the downfall of capitalism the world over,” a socialist leader predicted in 1906, speaking in Chicago at the annual convention of the Industrial Workers of the World (I.W.W.). Yet, that year, the German economist Werner Sombart asked, “Why is there no socialism in the United States?” There was socialism, of course, but less than he and others expected. One of Sombart’s explanations was that Americans hadn’t suffered the worst ravages of “late capitalism” (a term that he coined): “On the reefs of roast beef and apple pie socialistic Utopias of every sort are sent to their doom,” he wrote. Call it the Too Many Arby’s theory of the American left.

“This is our year,” Debs said in 1912. And it was, but it was also American socialism’s last good year until this year. After that election, the Socialist Party began losing members from both its left wing and its right. At its convention in May, the Socialist Party had formally disavowed sabotage as a labor tactic; as a result, it saw members defect to the saboteur-friendly I.W.W. In November, the Democrat Woodrow Wilson won the Presidency, and soon Democrats began accomplishing much of what socialists had pledged to do. Although they neither abolished the Senate nor held a constitutional convention, progressives achieved the ratification of four constitutional amendments between 1913 and 1920, two in 1913 alone. (The Sixteenth granted Congress the right to impose a federal income tax, and the Seventeenth provided for the direct election of senators.) Other reforms proposed in the Socialist Party’s 1912 platform and adopted by Democrats—minimum-wage laws, maximum-hour laws, the abolition of child labor, old-age pensions, and unemployment insurance—saw success in the states, and by the end of the New Deal had been achieved nationally; meanwhile, the Socialist Party withered.

That was due to forces within and without. In 1917, American socialists divided over the Bolshevik Revolution, with some becoming Communists, and the Socialist Party announced that it opposed America’s entrance into the war in Europe: “In support of capitalism, we will not willingly give a single life or a single dollar.” To suppress dissent, Congress passed the notorious Espionage and Sedition Acts, under whose terms hundreds of socialists, including Debs, were prosecuted for their opposition to the war. In 1920, Debs, still in prison, ran for President with the slogan “From the Jail House to the White House.” Five years later, he declared the Socialist Party “as near a corpse as a thing can be.” After Debs’s death, in 1926, Norman Thomas, a former Presbyterian minister, replaced him as the quadrennial Socialist Party candidate for President. In 1939, the Party opposed American entry into the Second World War, on the ground that it wasn’t a working-class revolution but merely a clash between rival imperialist powers. The sociologist Daniel Bell memorably described the Party’s leader speaking in Madison Square Garden at an America First Committee rally in 1941: “Behind him lay only the charnel house of American socialism.” By 1950, amid the rise of McCarthyism and the second Red Scare, according to Bell, “American socialism as a political and social fact had become simply a notation in the archives of history.”

Commentators then set about pawing through those archives. In postwar America, observers revisited Sombart’s question about why there had been so little socialism in the United States. Aside from America’s prosperity relative to Europe, the top answers, over the years, have included: the United States has no feudal past and has never had an established class system; the American political apparatus dooms all third parties; American socialists failed to ally with unions; Americans don’t like ideas that come from Europe; the government has suppressed the political rights and, especially, the free speech of socialists; the Democratic Party has used socialist ideas to win elections for Democrats; and socialists are their own worst enemies, insisting on strict ideological conformity. As the sociologist Seymour Martin Lipset and the political scientist Gary Marks once wrote, “Explanations of socialism’s weakness in America are as numerous as socialists were few.”

Bell himself attributed much of socialism’s demise to its notorious fractiousness (“For every two socialists there are always three political opinions”). But, more broadly, he was inclined to believe that American socialists “could never resolve but only straddle the basic issue of either accepting capitalist society, and seeking to transform it from within as the labor movement did, or becoming the sworn enemy of that society, like the communists.” This dilemma has not abated.

Socialism in the United States failed as a political party. But it succeeded in influencing American economic and social policy, not only during the Progressive and the New Deal eras but also under Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. This last era of influence owed a great deal to the socialist Michael Harrington, who had taken a vow of poverty when he joined Dorothy Day’s Catholic Worker Movement, became a Marxist in 1952, and served as a leader of the Young People’s Socialist League. By the end of the nineteen-fifties, he’d begun to devote his time to the civil-rights movement. In 1960, the Socialist Party neither nominated nor endorsed a candidate for the Presidency. Harrington explained, “American socialism must concentrate its efforts on the battle for political realignment, for the creation of a real second party that will unite labor, liberals, Negroes, and provide them with an instrument for principled debate and effective action.” His idea was that socialism could find a home in the Democratic Party, once “the Southern racists and certain other corruptive elements have been forced out of it.”

In 1958, Harrington was asked by an editor at the magazine Commentary if he’d write about poverty in America. What he produced led to queries from book publishers. He initially demurred but eventually agreed. The result, “The Other America,” came out in March, 1962. At a time when the country was said to be enjoying an age of affluence, Harrington drew attention to the millions of people living in poverty. The American poor needed, he said, “an American Dickens.”

Harrington never used the word “socialism” in “The Other America,” but Norman Thomas remarked that Harrington had “written a book which consciously or subconsciously, all of us Socialists have been waiting for.” Yet the book scarcely made an impact until Dwight Macdonald’s thirteen-thousand-word review for this magazine appeared in January of 1963. “Our Invisible Poor,” still the longest and perhaps the most important book review that The New Yorker has ever published, was searing, pointed, and urgent: it sought specific action. “The federal government is the only purposeful force . . . that can reduce the numbers of the poor and make their lives more bearable,” Macdonald wrote. Walter Heller, the chair of John F. Kennedy’s Council of Economic Advisers, read the review and reportedly gave a copy to the President, who began planning a policy that became, under his successor, the War on Poverty.

When Harrington was made the leader of the Socialist Party, in 1968, he was already America’s best-known socialist, which, as he liked to say (borrowing a gibe from William F. Buckley, Jr.), was “like being the tallest building in Topeka, Kansas.” The year he assumed the leadership of a party that he did not believe ought to be a party, Harrington published “Toward a Democratic Left: A Radical Program for a New Majority,” in which he called for a “majority party of the democratic Left” that might well “bear an old label: the Democratic Party.” In 1972, Harrington resigned as co-chairman of the Socialist Party, and the next year he helped form what would be called, by 1982, the Democratic Socialists of America.

After years of slow growth, the D.S.A.’s membership began expanding in fits and starts following Sanders’s Presidential bid in 2016. “America will never be a socialist country,” Donald Trump said in his State of the Union address in 2019. But popular support for socialism, and for positions held by democratic socialists like Sanders and Mamdani, has surged since Trump’s reëlection. This fall, a Gallup survey found that public approval of socialism had reached a new high of forty-three per cent, and that backing for key measures endorsed by the D.S.A. had surged, too: two-thirds of Americans support Medicare for All.

Socialism has been strongest in the United States during eras of high inequality and has been weakest during eras of shared prosperity. The share of income going to the top one per cent began climbing in the nineteen-seventies and has risen to levels last seen in the nineteen-twenties. There may still be, here and there, reefs of roast beef and apple pie, but the same cannot be said of affordable medical care, housing, or higher education. Democrats of the Progressive Era fought for and achieved labor legislation, campaign-finance reform, social-welfare provisions, and anti-monopoly measures. Democrats from Bill Clinton to Joe Biden have not been half as successful. Hence the Sanders insurgency in 2016, and the prominence of the D.S.A. today. But is a new New Left—what Harrington called the Next Left—really emerging? And, if it is, what is its plan?

Socialists, who advocate central planning of the economy, are strangely ambivalent about issuing plans. Marx himself cautioned against “writing recipes” for “the cook-shops of the future,” but he did imagine what a day without capitalism and the division of labor would look like—a day when people could do whatever they wanted. You could, Marx mused, “hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticize after dinner.”

Writing nearly a century later, the economist John Maynard Keynes, a liberal sympathetic to socialism, similarly imagined a future requiring very little labor, a “destination of economic bliss” that, he warned, would produce a new problem: “how to occupy the leisure, which science and compound interest will have won.”

In “Toward a Democratic Left,” Harrington took pains to insist that his ideas ought not to be taken as “blueprints.” But in recent years democratic socialists have not shied away from socialist solutionism. In “The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World,” an economist, a philosopher, and the founder of the magazine Jacobin propose a model for a just society and ask readers to imagine a day in a socialist future: “Some people may spend more time reading Russian novels or cooking elaborate meals with people they love or hiking and camping in nature.”

It’s no surprise, then, that the D.S.A.’s 2026 platform also asks Americans to imagine a day off in a world without capitalism. “Maybe in the morning, you walk your kids to school, run errands, or go to a doctor’s appointment. In the afternoon, you might play a sport, practice a new skill, read, plan a trip. In the evening, you could meet up with friends or family and eat together, maybe go to the movies or down to the park.”

If all this sounds oddly familiar, that’s because it’s the kind of future that Elon Musk and Sam Altman like to talk about, a world of abundance in a planned economy in which poverty has been eliminated and wage labor curtailed. In the twenty-first century, the belief that socialism is destiny has begun to converge with the belief that artificial intelligence is destiny. (A planned economy is far likelier, after all, in an economy run by artificial intelligence than in any future imagined in “Das Kapital,” even if the prospects for human freedom are, alas, far worse.) These days, you can find A.I. boosters repurposing rhetoric once championed by Eugene Debs. “Quit being a wage slave,” one A.I. marketing service tells potential clients. “Stop building their dreams. Replace labor with AI systems.”

What will people do all day in an A.I. future? According to tech titans, there will be no need to do anything—you’ll be paid a universal basic income, or, as Musk likes to call it, a “universal ‘you can have whatever you want’ income.” Altman has proposed that instead of universal basic income people might be given “universal basic compute,” which they can use, sell, or donate. “You own part of the productivity!” he has said, sounding like Marx. Altman is sure that in this future “we’ll find stuff to do that we really care about.” Musk likens working in this future to growing vegetables even though you can buy them at the store. “Some people still do it because they like growing vegetables,” he says.

The fullest statement of this world view is the philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2024 book, “Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World.” It begins with a Marxian joke about how Bostrom made his fortune by writing a “recipe book.” He is best known for his 2014 book, “Superintelligence,” which warned of the coming A.I. apocalypse. In “Deep Utopia,” though, he imagines a post-scarcity, post-work utopia whose chief problem is “the purpose problem,” which he meditates on for some five hundred pages that constitute nothing so much as an illustration of his own attempt to find some purpose . . . by writing a meandering book of random, self-indulgent musings about purposelessness.

For socialists in 2026, as for socialists in 1912, absorption into the Democratic Party risks trading the ambition to replace capitalism for the more modest goal of reforming it. But this time around there’s a strange new twist: the convergence of socialist determinism with technological determinism, Marxism become Muskism. The Democratic Party may well advance socialism’s most practical and urgent demands: Medicare for All, a Green New Deal. But Silicon Valley, with more power than any political party, seems keen to turn socialism’s most extravagant dream into a nightmare: a world in which people no longer have to do anything, because they are no longer needed.

It has much in common with the Socialist Party platform of 1912.

“We are workers fighting to transform society: to win the battle for democracy, draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic,” the program pledges, while inveighing against the existing parties: “Both are funded by the same criminal class of billionaires and war profiteers.” The program proposes, among other things, the abolition of the Senate and the replacement of the Presidency and Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress.
A number of prominent Democrats condemned the platform. On Fox News, the host Shannon Bream asked Megan Romer, a D.S.A. co-chair, to confirm some of its proposals:
Romer, who grinned and seemed almost to laugh at one point during this quiz, came across as glib and, at best, remarkably naïve. “These people are insane,” Ted Cruz tweeted.

Then came Election Day, an epic Democratic sweep that reinvigorated the Party and brought gains for socialists not seen since 1912. Six D.S.A. members—from California, Colorado, Michigan, New York, and Pennsylvania—won seats in Congress (and the two sitting D.S.A. members won reëlection). D.S.A. candidates won mayoral races in Los Angeles; Washington, D.C.; Ann Arbor, Michigan; and Providence, Rhode Island. Even socialism’s losses were triumphs. The little red scare of 2026 backfired. The D.S.A. member Angie Nixon lost her long-shot bid to unseat the Republican Ashley Moody, a U.S. senator from Florida, who had characterized the campaign as “freedom versus socialism,” but Moody’s margin of victory was just 2.9 per cent. Mamdani, speaking at the Election Night party of Kathy Hochul (no socialist she), announced the dawn of a new era: “We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again.”

The United States has no meaningful socialist party, and socialism has never overtaken either of the country’s two major political parties. This distinguishes the U.S. from every other Western democracy and would have surprised early American socialists, who pointed to a tradition of communalism stretching from the Shakers to the Owenites. In 1869, John Humphrey Noyes, the American preacher and utopian, proclaimed that “this country has been from the beginning, and especially for the last forty years, a laboratory in which Socialisms of all kinds have been experimenting.” It was as if socialism was in the soil, as American as the Revolution.

Nevertheless, socialism didn’t really come to the fore of American politics until the Panic of 1893, when, according to Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., “a vague terror went over the earth and the word socialism began to be heard.” After the railway magnate George Pullman cut workers’ wages by a quarter, Debs called for a strike, and in 1895 he was sent to prison for his role in organizing it; Victor Berger visited him, bringing a copy of “Das Kapital.” (Debs’s extraordinary life is the subject of a lively and admiring new biography, “American Socialist,” by Shawn Gude.) Debs, a Democrat, said that he had previously “heard but little of Socialism,” and he did not become a socialist until 1897, after a campaign funded by plutocrats elevated William McKinley to the White House, convincing Debs that the rich controlled politics. “Money constitutes no proper basis of civilization,” he concluded. He first ran for President in 1900, and when he ran again four years later he earned more than four times as many votes.

“If my reading of history is correct, the prophecy of Marx will be fulfilled, and America will ring the downfall of capitalism the world over,” a socialist leader predicted in 1906, speaking in Chicago at the annual convention of the Industrial Workers of the World (I.W.W.). Yet, that year, the German economist Werner Sombart asked, “Why is there no socialism in the United States?” There was socialism, of course, but less than he and others expected. One of Sombart’s explanations was that Americans hadn’t suffered the worst ravages of “late capitalism” (a term that he coined): “On the reefs of roast beef and apple pie socialistic Utopias of every sort are sent to their doom,” he wrote. Call it the Too Many Arby’s theory of the American left.

“This is our year,” Debs said in 1912. And it was, but it was also American socialism’s last good year until this year. After that election, the Socialist Party began losing members from both its left wing and its right. At its convention in May, the Socialist Party had formally disavowed sabotage as a labor tactic; as a result, it saw members defect to the saboteur-friendly I.W.W. In November, the Democrat Woodrow Wilson won the Presidency, and soon Democrats began accomplishing much of what socialists had pledged to do. Although they neither abolished the Senate nor held a constitutional convention, progressives achieved the ratification of four constitutional amendments between 1913 and 1920, two in 1913 alone. (The Sixteenth granted Congress the right to impose a federal income tax, and the Seventeenth provided for the direct election of senators.) Other reforms proposed in the Socialist Party’s 1912 platform and adopted by Democrats—minimum-wage laws, maximum-hour laws, the abolition of child labor, old-age pensions, and unemployment insurance—saw success in the states, and by the end of the New Deal had been achieved nationally; meanwhile, the Socialist Party withered.

That was due to forces within and without. In 1917, American socialists divided over the Bolshevik Revolution, with some becoming Communists, and the Socialist Party announced that it opposed America’s entrance into the war in Europe: “In support of capitalism, we will not willingly give a single life or a single dollar.” To suppress dissent, Congress passed the notorious Espionage and Sedition Acts, under whose terms hundreds of socialists, including Debs, were prosecuted for their opposition to the war. In 1920, Debs, still in prison, ran for President with the slogan “From the Jail House to the White House.” Five years later, he declared the Socialist Party “as near a corpse as a thing can be.” After Debs’s death, in 1926, Norman Thomas, a former Presbyterian minister, replaced him as the quadrennial Socialist Party candidate for President. In 1939, the Party opposed American entry into the Second World War, on the ground that it wasn’t a working-class revolution but merely a clash between rival imperialist powers. The sociologist Daniel Bell memorably described the Party’s leader speaking in Madison Square Garden at an America First Committee rally in 1941: “Behind him lay only the charnel house of American socialism.” By 1950, amid the rise of McCarthyism and the second Red Scare, according to Bell, “American socialism as a political and social fact had become simply a notation in the archives of history.”

Commentators then set about pawing through those archives. In postwar America, observers revisited Sombart’s question about why there had been so little socialism in the United States. Aside from America’s prosperity relative to Europe, the top answers, over the years, have included: the United States has no feudal past and has never had an established class system; the American political apparatus dooms all third parties; American socialists failed to ally with unions; Americans don’t like ideas that come from Europe; the government has suppressed the political rights and, especially, the free speech of socialists; the Democratic Party has used socialist ideas to win elections for Democrats; and socialists are their own worst enemies, insisting on strict ideological conformity. As the sociologist Seymour Martin Lipset and the political scientist Gary Marks once wrote, “Explanations of socialism’s weakness in America are as numerous as socialists were few.”

Bell himself attributed much of socialism’s demise to its notorious fractiousness (“For every two socialists there are always three political opinions”). But, more broadly, he was inclined to believe that American socialists “could never resolve but only straddle the basic issue of either accepting capitalist society, and seeking to transform it from within as the labor movement did, or becoming the sworn enemy of that society, like the communists.” This dilemma has not abated.

Socialism in the United States failed as a political party. But it succeeded in influencing American economic and social policy, not only during the Progressive and the New Deal eras but also under Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. This last era of influence owed a great deal to the socialist Michael Harrington, who had taken a vow of poverty when he joined Dorothy Day’s Catholic Worker Movement, became a Marxist in 1952, and served as a leader of the Young People’s Socialist League. By the end of the nineteen-fifties, he’d begun to devote his time to the civil-rights movement. In 1960, the Socialist Party neither nominated nor endorsed a candidate for the Presidency. Harrington explained, “American socialism must concentrate its efforts on the battle for political realignment, for the creation of a real second party that will unite labor, liberals, Negroes, and provide them with an instrument for principled debate and effective action.” His idea was that socialism could find a home in the Democratic Party, once “the Southern racists and certain other corruptive elements have been forced out of it.”

In 1958, Harrington was asked by an editor at the magazine Commentary if he’d write about poverty in America. What he produced led to queries from book publishers. He initially demurred but eventually agreed. The result, “The Other America,” came out in March, 1962. At a time when the country was said to be enjoying an age of affluence, Harrington drew attention to the millions of people living in poverty. The American poor needed, he said, “an American Dickens.”

Harrington never used the word “socialism” in “The Other America,” but Norman Thomas remarked that Harrington had “written a book which consciously or subconsciously, all of us Socialists have been waiting for.” Yet the book scarcely made an impact until Dwight Macdonald’s thirteen-thousand-word review for this magazine appeared in January of 1963. “Our Invisible Poor,” still the longest and perhaps the most important book review that The New Yorker has ever published, was searing, pointed, and urgent: it sought specific action. “The federal government is the only purposeful force . . . that can reduce the numbers of the poor and make their lives more bearable,” Macdonald wrote. Walter Heller, the chair of John F. Kennedy’s Council of Economic Advisers, read the review and reportedly gave a copy to the President, who began planning a policy that became, under his successor, the War on Poverty.

When Harrington was made the leader of the Socialist Party, in 1968, he was already America’s best-known socialist, which, as he liked to say (borrowing a gibe from William F. Buckley, Jr.), was “like being the tallest building in Topeka, Kansas.” The year he assumed the leadership of a party that he did not believe ought to be a party, Harrington published “Toward a Democratic Left: A Radical Program for a New Majority,” in which he called for a “majority party of the democratic Left” that might well “bear an old label: the Democratic Party.” In 1972, Harrington resigned as co-chairman of the Socialist Party, and the next year he helped form what would be called, by 1982, the Democratic Socialists of America.

After years of slow growth, the D.S.A.’s membership began expanding in fits and starts following Sanders’s Presidential bid in 2016. “America will never be a socialist country,” Donald Trump said in his State of the Union address in 2019. But popular support for socialism, and for positions held by democratic socialists like Sanders and Mamdani, has surged since Trump’s reëlection. This fall, a Gallup survey found that public approval of socialism had reached a new high of forty-three per cent, and that backing for key measures endorsed by the D.S.A. had surged, too: two-thirds of Americans support Medicare for All.

Socialism has been strongest in the United States during eras of high inequality and has been weakest during eras of shared prosperity. The share of income going to the top one per cent began climbing in the nineteen-seventies and has risen to levels last seen in the nineteen-twenties. There may still be, here and there, reefs of roast beef and apple pie, but the same cannot be said of affordable medical care, housing, or higher education. Democrats of the Progressive Era fought for and achieved labor legislation, campaign-finance reform, social-welfare provisions, and anti-monopoly measures. Democrats from Bill Clinton to Joe Biden have not been half as successful. Hence the Sanders insurgency in 2016, and the prominence of the D.S.A. today. But is a new New Left—what Harrington called the Next Left—really emerging? And, if it is, what is its plan?

Socialists, who advocate central planning of the economy, are strangely ambivalent about issuing plans. Marx himself cautioned against “writing recipes” for “the cook-shops of the future,” but he did imagine what a day without capitalism and the division of labor would look like—a day when people could do whatever they wanted. You could, Marx mused, “hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticize after dinner.”

Writing nearly a century later, the economist John Maynard Keynes, a liberal sympathetic to socialism, similarly imagined a future requiring very little labor, a “destination of economic bliss” that, he warned, would produce a new problem: “how to occupy the leisure, which science and compound interest will have won.”

In “Toward a Democratic Left,” Harrington took pains to insist that his ideas ought not to be taken as “blueprints.” But in recent years democratic socialists have not shied away from socialist solutionism. In “The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World,” an economist, a philosopher, and the founder of the magazine Jacobin propose a model for a just society and ask readers to imagine a day in a socialist future: “Some people may spend more time reading Russian novels or cooking elaborate meals with people they love or hiking and camping in nature.”

It’s no surprise, then, that the D.S.A.’s 2026 platform also asks Americans to imagine a day off in a world without capitalism. “Maybe in the morning, you walk your kids to school, run errands, or go to a doctor’s appointment. In the afternoon, you might play a sport, practice a new skill, read, plan a trip. In the evening, you could meet up with friends or family and eat together, maybe go to the movies or down to the park.”

If all this sounds oddly familiar, that’s because it’s the kind of future that Elon Musk and Sam Altman like to talk about, a world of abundance in a planned economy in which poverty has been eliminated and wage labor curtailed. In the twenty-first century, the belief that socialism is destiny has begun to converge with the belief that artificial intelligence is destiny. (A planned economy is far likelier, after all, in an economy run by artificial intelligence than in any future imagined in “Das Kapital,” even if the prospects for human freedom are, alas, far worse.) These days, you can find A.I. boosters repurposing rhetoric once championed by Eugene Debs. “Quit being a wage slave,” one A.I. marketing service tells potential clients. “Stop building their dreams. Replace labor with AI systems.”

What will people do all day in an A.I. future? According to tech titans, there will be no need to do anything—you’ll be paid a universal basic income, or, as Musk likes to call it, a “universal ‘you can have whatever you want’ income.” Altman has proposed that instead of universal basic income people might be given “universal basic compute,” which they can use, sell, or donate. “You own part of the productivity!” he has said, sounding like Marx. Altman is sure that in this future “we’ll find stuff to do that we really care about.” Musk likens working in this future to growing vegetables even though you can buy them at the store. “Some people still do it because they like growing vegetables,” he says.

The fullest statement of this world view is the philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2024 book, “Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World.” It begins with a Marxian joke about how Bostrom made his fortune by writing a “recipe book.” He is best known for his 2014 book, “Superintelligence,” which warned of the coming A.I. apocalypse. In “Deep Utopia,” though, he imagines a post-scarcity, post-work utopia whose chief problem is “the purpose problem,” which he meditates on for some five hundred pages that constitute nothing so much as an illustration of his own attempt to find some purpose . . . by writing a meandering book of random, self-indulgent musings about purposelessness.

For socialists in 2026, as for socialists in 1912, absorption into the Democratic Party risks trading the ambition to replace capitalism for the more modest goal of reforming it. But this time around there’s a strange new twist: the convergence of socialist determinism with technological determinism, Marxism become Muskism. The Democratic Party may well advance socialism’s most practical and urgent demands: Medicare for All, a Green New Deal. But Silicon Valley, with more power than any political party, seems keen to turn socialism’s most extravagant dream into a nightmare: a world in which people no longer have to do anything, because they are no longer needed.

articles.title: What It Takes to Save a Town from Wildfire
articles.author: Eric Klinenberg
articles.body_markdown:
In 1991, when the city of Boulder asked Larry Donner to become its fire chief, he couldn’t believe his luck. A Denver native, Donner was forty-two and working as the fire chief of Iowa City. He and his wife, Susan Loo, missed the natural beauty of the Rocky Mountains: rolling meadows, colorful wildflowers, dense forests, rushing creeks. They also missed the outdoor adventures and the community that came with them.

The kinds of outdoor adventures that Donner would contend with as fire chief, though, were stressful and dangerous—wildfires, damaging winds, flash floods—and Loo insisted that they find a home in a relatively safe area. “I didn’t want Larry worrying about his own house when there was an emergency,” she told me in September as the two of them sat at their dining-room table in bluejeans and T-shirts, casual as weekday hikers. They settled in Louisville, a pleasant suburb about nine miles southeast of Boulder, surrounded by open grasslands. “We’re miles from the foothills where the forest fires happen,” explained Donner, now seventy-seven and retired, with thin gray hair, glasses, and skin marbled by the fierce Colorado sun. “I figured it was safe.”

Over the years, Donner worked hard to make his house fire-resistant. “I put in James Hardie board siding”—made of a noncombustible fibre-cement composite—“and a Class A fire-rated roof. I took a wood deck off the back, cleared out vegetation, and built a flagstone area next to the house. We had two giant spruce trees on the property that I just couldn’t cut down, but otherwise I thought I’d done everything.” In Boulder, he led a campaign in 1994 to ban wood shingles on new construction. “When you get a fire, they burn,” he said, “and in high winds they’re like Frisbees, flying torches.”

For thirty years, as Boulder endured major fires and floods, Donner’s home remained untouched. But, in 2021, the weather turned. The grasses grew four or five feet during a wet spring, and, after a dry fall, the result was “like a field of matchsticks, chest high,” Donner said. The meadows that historically buffered his home, protecting it from wildfires, had now turned into fuel.

On December 30th, a powerful windstorm swept down the Front Range foothills, with sustained winds in excess of forty-five miles an hour and gusts of up to a hundred. They rekindled a controlled debris fire on property occupied by Twelve Tribes, a fundamentalist Christian sect. Another fire was ignited by arcing power lines near the Marshall Mesa trailhead. At 11:05 A.M. , the Boulder County Sheriff’s Office dispatched firefighters to a conflagration spreading across dry grassland, fuelled by every shingle and shed in its path. The Marshall Fire, as it became known, rapidly consumed structures, advancing east at what Donner described as “the speed of wind.”

At 11:47 A.M. , authorities issued the first evacuation orders, expanding them continuously as hurricane-force winds projected airborne embers ahead of a roughly half-mile front across wide streets and even across a multi-lane highway near Donner’s development. “Once you get an urban conflagration, there’s really nothing you can do to stop it,” Donner told me. “Now the fuel isn’t just grassland. It’s every house that catches fire, sending heat and flames and flying embers to the houses next to them. No water system is designed to handle an urban conflagration. It just collapses, and all you can do is pray.”

Donner and Loo say they saw the fire approach their neighborhood long before they received an evacuation order. They grabbed a few cherished items and drove to a relative’s home, where they turned on the TV. “I could see our house burning behind the reporter,” Donner recounted. “I’d been worried about the spruce trees catching, but they were fine. The problem was I hadn’t put ember shields on our vents. I needed about one-eighth-inch wire mesh to cover attic vents, which I could have gotten at Home Depot.” Without that, embers got into the attic. “Our house burned top down, then inside out.”

By the time the winds died, the Marshall Fire had destroyed more than a thousand structures and shattered communities. Donner and Loo lost nearly everything. Luckier neighbors, including a woman named Peggy Driscoll, returned to standing homes, but they were so saturated with smoke and soot that disaster-mitigation companies, after peeling them like onions for months, deemed them uninhabitable.

“Look around,” Driscoll told me at her rebuilt mountain-modern-style house in unincorporated Boulder County. “It’s the suburbs. I’d always thought of wildfires as forest fires, and, since we’re not the typical landscape that burns, I didn’t think we were at risk.”

The Marshall Fire showed that the danger of wildfires is broader and more serious than most people realize. Once wildfires reach dense residential areas, their spread resembles that of infectious diseases: no household can be fully protected unless surrounding properties are protected, too.

“If you want your home to survive, you need to have herd immunity,” Jennifer Balch, a fire ecologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder, told me as we walked through her neighborhood, steps from a stunning mountain trail that’s rich with fire fuels in the fall. Dressed in the form-fitting athleisure endemic to the city, Balch explained that her community sits in the wildland-urban interface, or wui (pronounced “woo-ee”), where fire risk is highest. “I do get nervous when it’s hot, dry, and windy,” she said, brushing her curly blond hair from her eyes. “As you can see, we’re pretty far from herd immunity here.”

For much of the past century, urban conflagrations seemed, like polio or measles, a scourge that science and government had conquered. Modernized fire departments, safer building materials, hydrants, and building codes had largely eliminated catastrophes like the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. But, by the nineteen-nineties, housing developments were spreading into forests and grasslands increasingly parched by climate change, bringing structure-to-structure fires back. The 2018 Camp Fire, in Paradise, California; the 2023 Lahaina Fire, on Maui; and the 2025 Palisades and Eaton Fires were devastating examples. Communities abroad face similar dangers, from Australia’s bushfire-prone suburbs to parts of Europe, Asia, and South America.

Some residents whose homes were engulfed by fire understood that they lived on a combustible landscape; others were surprised. Balch, the ecologist, spent a decade building a data set that combined satellite information about the speed and spread of more than sixty thousand American wildfires from 2001 to 2020 with daily incident-command reports from fire-suppression teams, and two hundred million housing and property records. “The trends are remarkable,” she told me as we walked through the foothills near her neighborhood, grass crunching beneath our feet. “Here’s the main thing: Forget megafires. It’s fast fires that do the most damage.” Balch and her colleagues reported in Science that, among the conflagrations in their database, fast fires—those growing by more than sixteen hundred and twenty hectares on any single day—made up less than three per cent of the total but accounted for almost ninety per cent of the structures damaged or destroyed.

Another Science paper, by a team led by Volker Radeloff, an ecologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, reports that from 1990 to 2020 the number of American homes in the wui increased by forty-six per cent, from thirty million to forty-four million. Although most U.S. regions are vulnerable to destructive conflagrations, Balch’s data show that such fires are becoming more prevalent—and much faster—in the West, where the average maximum daily growth of wildfire area increased by two hundred and fifty per cent between 2001 and 2020. “In California, it’s four hundred per cent,” she told me. “If you have a house there, that’s a terrifying fact.”

Among the first institutions to recognize this change was the insurance industry, on which the modern housing market rests. By the nineteenth century, American mortgage lenders commonly required borrowers to carry fire insurance. During the New Deal, the federal government began insuring mortgage lenders against losses when borrowers defaulted, adding a second layer of protection. Together, these arrangements became foundational to American homeownership.

In the twenty-first century, extreme weather has cracked that foundation. A hotter and more violent climate, combined with runaway development in high-risk areas, has helped make billion-dollar disasters more common. Soaring claims have been accompanied by soaring premiums. Meanwhile, insurers have increasingly exercised their option not to renew existing policies. For growing numbers of Americans, the insurance required for a mortgage is prohibitively expensive. In high-risk areas, it may be available only through state-run residual markets, including Fair Access to Insurance Requirements ( FAIR ) plans, which often come with high prices and limited benefits.

Insurers have long sought to reduce risk by rewarding safety measures such as smoke alarms and security cameras. More recently, actuaries, policymakers, and fire experts have explored ways to do the same on a community-wide scale. Among them is Nancy Watkins, a property-and-casualty-insurance actuary at the global consultancy Milliman, who has had struggles with her own homeowners’-insurance coverage, in California.

“I loved that old policy,” she said wistfully, as if recalling a beloved pet. But her insurer pulled out of the state, and the one she turned to next decided not to renew about half its policies in the area, including hers. We sat in her yard in Orinda, over the hills from Oakland, amid oak, redwood, maple, and lemon trees, overlooking dry grassland. “The chief actuary of another company told me, ‘Orinda is my worst nightmare,’ because we have so many high-value homes in a small area with terrible access, twisty roads, lots of overgrown vegetation, and very little mitigation. It’s so beautiful, but when I drive through these hills, I often think, Wow, an insurer could lose a lot of money here.”

Watkins, who is sixty-five, has a mild Southern drawl, purple-dyed hair, and an analytic mind that eventually forced her to confront the fire risk she had long downplayed in her personal life, despite her professional expertise. Her husband led their local “Firewise” group, part of a National Fire Protection Association program that helps residents and neighborhoods organize around wildfire resistance. “He had been telling me for years that we should clear five feet around our house,” she said. “But we’d spent a lot of money on landscaping, and I liked it. I didn’t want to make the change.” She and her husband had invested heavily in her “California dream home,” but now they needed a better option than the state’s FAIR plan. “That’s when we decided to do the mitigation makeover.”

There are two main ways to protect a home from fire. The first, “hardening,” replaces vulnerable building components, such as single-pane windows and vinyl gutters, with fire-resistant alternatives, such as double-pane, double-tempered windows and metal gutters. The second, creating “defensible space,” clears combustible material from the perimeter, particularly “Zone Zero,” the five feet closest to the building.
